archive_12_001.speaker: narrator
archive_12_001.text: The reading afternoon began as a problem of stools. The lower school owned twelve, the village assembly room could lend eight and the teacher expected twenty-seven people if snow left the local path open. Luo asked which people were children and which adults would mind standing. The teacher said she would ask rather than guess. By the seventy-ninth morning, the plan had changed to two small sittings in the checked village room. Sun liked the second sitting better, when she could listen before deciding whether to read her own fish aloud.

archive_12_002.speaker: narrator
archive_12_002.text: The teacher came with a worn purse containing the school reading group's four copper, collected earlier for its winter programme. Three would pay Sun for the agreed appearance; one would cover the room attendant's additional hour. Tea would be the school's own kettle and dry fuel, brought by its cook, while visitors could bring cups or drink plain water. Dai approved the archive's loan of six public reference copies for the specific afternoon, listing their condition and return time. She did not offer the archive's winter kitchen as a convenient extension of every good village intention.

archive_12_003.speaker: narrator
archive_12_003.text: Sun wanted the teacher to tell listeners that the fish story was new. People sometimes treated the date beneath an old woman's name as the day somebody had found an old manuscript. The teacher wrote a large line beneath the title: composed this winter. Sun asked for her name immediately underneath, in lettering people could see from the back stool. Luo thought the insistence excessive until he remembered the class book's confusion. He then offered to hold the board while the teacher wrote, and managed to smear the corner with his thumb.

archive_12_004.speaker: sun_nian
archive_12_004.text: You may keep that thumb mark. It proves somebody alive was holding the board while somebody else wrote it. You must not call it my signature or pay a scholar to say it shows the vigour of my late style. If the board becomes famous, Luo may claim the corner. I claim the fish. The child claims her snail, if she wants to bring it. We can inhabit the same afternoon without placing all our words beneath the oldest person's name.

archive_12_005.speaker: narrator
archive_12_005.text: The child arrived with her mother and three revised lines. Her snail no longer waited for the fish to invite it beneath the roof. It asked the owner first, a change the teacher had suggested after their lesson on ordinary courtesies. Sun said the first version had been more surprising. The child said surprise was not the only reason to tell a story. Neither woman corrected the other into agreement. The teacher marked the revision as the child's present choice and asked whether she wanted to read, have someone else read, or leave the page at home.

archive_12_006.speaker: narrator
archive_12_006.text: The card seller had obtained the child's permission and her mother's approval for twenty separate snail cards, paying three copper under a small written agreement. Their limited printing and credit belonged to that agreement, not to Sun's sixty-card licence. The child asked whether she could give her own copy away. The seller said yes, then explained that giving away one card did not instruct him to print another hundred. Her mother asked what happened to unsold cards after the stated selling period. He produced the deadline and return option before anyone had to invent a dispute.

archive_12_007.speaker: narrator
archive_12_007.text: On the eightieth morning the seller brought his first finished fish cards to the archive. He carried them inside a cloth-lined box and looked proud of the clean paper edges. Sun looked first at her name. The printer had placed it in a tiny line beneath a much larger shop heading. The seller opened the agreement, saw the words about prominent credit and stopped explaining how difficult the road had been. He said the layout failed the term he had signed. His pride turned into the anxious calculation of a man with sixty pieces of unsold stock.

archive_12_008.speaker: narrator
archive_12_008.text: Tan examined the sheet without touching its clean face. The printer had left enough blank margin for an added credit strip, but the strip would have to stay attached through ordinary handling and be visibly part of the edition. Sun did not want her name falling off into someone's tea. Dai asked whether relabelling would satisfy her agreement or whether she wanted the seller to withdraw the run. The seller waited for her answer. His need to recover printing costs mattered; it did not silently revise the prominence he had promised.

archive_12_009.speaker: narrator
archive_12_009.text: Sun asked to see one corrected specimen before answering for the run. Tan proposed an ordinary paper strip attached along its clean margin with the printer's proper paste, tested after drying. She refused any treatment which made a printed card pretend to be an untouched original manuscript. The seller agreed to a clearly labelled correction. The archive would neither lend its certification mark nor charge its winter work fund for the shop's mistake. Tan could give a brief inspection within her paid public advice hours, then the printer needed to do the work.

archive_12_010.speaker: narrator
archive_12_010.text: Yue watched the seller carry his box downstairs. She had expected him to become argumentative when money entered the conversation. Instead he asked whether Sun would permit an apology on the correction slip, or whether that would burden the story with his failure. Sun said one sentence on the shop notice was enough. She wanted children to meet the fish, not spend their afternoon learning his printer's excuses. He laughed at that, somewhat painfully. She laughed back. The disagreement had not made either of them a different species of person.

archive_12_011.speaker: narrator
archive_12_011.text: The teacher's next difficulty concerned the price. Two families had said they could attend but could not buy a card. She asked the seller for a cheaper school bundle. He showed her his paper and printing bill, then pointed to the already paid authors' fees. A lower price for every copy would leave him without the agreed work margin. Luo started to suggest an archive subsidy before the teacher reminded him that its free reference copies already allowed pupils to read. Owning a card and hearing a story were different opportunities, though both could matter.

archive_12_012.speaker: narrator
archive_12_012.text: They agreed that the school would retain its permitted teaching copy, and the seller would offer two visibly marked imperfect-margin fish cards at a lower price after the credit repair had passed. The defects were in the trimming, not the text; Sun saw and approved their description. Nobody would sell a child's work cheaply because its author was small. Families could also copy a short permitted passage for their own learning under the stated classroom terms. The teacher put those options on the announcement without promising that every reader would leave with a purchased sheet.

archive_12_013.speaker: narrator
archive_12_013.text: At the residential supper table on day eighty, the cook entered one extra food share for He Xi's and his mother's visiting bowls. He said carrying a card home could feel like proof that an occasion belonged to oneself. His mother asked whether he remembered every feast by buying its bowl. He said no, but she had cooked those feasts. The cook asked whether nobody else's work made a memory. He flushed and admitted he had made a grand theory from wanting a card. His mother reached for her own earned purse.

archive_12_014.speaker: narrator
archive_12_014.text: The exchange did not end with the adults declaring him grateful. His mother brought out the small purse from her paid kitchen shifts and said she could choose to buy something which had no practical use. That choice did not make her wages a family fund available whenever he felt embarrassed. He asked what she wanted. She wanted the imperfect fish card, because the fish's neighbour was plainly the sort of person who borrowed bowls and returned advice. He offered to collect it on his route after she had paid. This time he named the ordinary collection charge.

archive_12_015.speaker: narrator
archive_12_015.text: Luo tried the reading aloud in the village room on day eighty-one. Its low ceiling returned his own voice too quickly, and he had to slow down so the last words did not cover the next sentence. The attendant moved the back stools after checking the floor beneath their legs. A loose tread at the entrance was marked and blocked until the owner's carpenter secured it. Sun inspected the distance from her chair to the nearest bench, then said she wanted a table to rest the page rather than holding it up like a proclamation.

archive_12_016.speaker: narrator
archive_12_016.text: The carpenter completed the tread before the afternoon's rehearsal resumed. The room owner paid for her own entrance repair; it did not become a hidden use of the archive's supply order. He Xi checked the cleared local route and wrote the actual turn near the lamp shop on the invitation map. Its broad arrow avoided the little shortcut he liked using alone. The teacher kept a cancellation line for heavy snow or a renewed ice warning. She said she had already promised the pupils a story, and could tell it at school later if the path made this room unwise.

archive_12_017.speaker: narrator
archive_12_017.text: A pupil asked whether the fish could predict rain. Sun said the fish had been very bad at predicting rain and rather good at selling other creatures the impression that it knew. The pupil asked whether that meant the fish was a custodian. Dai, who had come to check the borrowed reference copies, waited while the room went quiet. Sun said a fish could resemble several professions on different days. Dai asked whether the sequel included a fish learning to read the weather board. The pupil said that might cost another card.

archive_12_018.speaker: narrator
archive_12_018.text: By evening, the corrected specimen had dried at the printer's shop. Its added author strip remained secure under normal bending and handling, without covering the original text or implying archive endorsement. Sun accepted that visible correction for the licensed run. The seller retained a dated account of the faulty layout and repaired the run at his own expense. He would bring the sixty corrected cards before the reading. Sun signed only for the remedy she had actually inspected. The bright new name across the margin pleased her more than she had expected.

archive_12_019.speaker: narrator
archive_12_019.text: A new snow warning arrived before dawn on the eighty-second day. The local watcher had marked the village path safe for morning walking but expected drifting by late afternoon. The teacher shortened both sittings and moved the second earlier, then contacted the families on the local loop before they started out. People beyond that checked loop were told to wait for the school reading instead. Luo disliked shrinking an event so carefully prepared. Sun said it was still an event if nobody had to become its brave survivor on the way home.

archive_12_020.speaker: narrator
archive_12_020.text: Yue walked down with the borrowed reference copies after Tan checked their lined carrier. Her ordinary calf movement stayed quiet on the cleared path; the carrying load sat within the usual light assignment. He Xi walked ahead to the marked turn, where the attendant had spread grit before the doorway. A small girl arrived wearing two different mittens and announced that one belonged to yesterday. The teacher answered that today would accept it. Inside, the stools smelled faintly of the assembly room's old varnish, and the first listeners chose places without being arranged into a perfect picture.

archive_12_021.speaker: narrator
archive_12_021.text: The seller set his repaired cards on a separate table near the exit. The reading could be heard without passing through his sales queue. Sun placed her own large manuscript page on the speaking table and adjusted her glasses. Dai remained near the back beside the reference carrier, apparently absorbed in its fastening. Luo moved the youngest stool so its occupant could see around a tall man's shoulder. The child with the snail sat beside her mother, looking so fiercely at her page that Yue wondered whether the words might get frightened and leave.

archive_12_022.speaker: narrator
archive_12_022.text: The teacher introduced the two authors by their chosen names and dates. She then showed the permitted reference copy which had supported the school's older fable lessons, carefully distinguishing it from today's new fish. A listener asked why a reading needed so much paper work. The teacher answered that it needed less than a later quarrel over whose story had sold the cards. She did not read the contracts aloud. She gave enough context for the names to make sense, then stepped aside so Sun could begin without her life becoming the introduction.

archive_12_023.speaker: narrator
archive_12_023.text: Sun's voice was quieter than Luo's and much less obedient to the room. At first people leaned forward to catch the line about the fish's shiny rain hat. Then she paused, looked up and repeated it with such solemn foolishness that the back bench laughed. The fish promised a dry day to the creatures who paid first, a wet day to those who paid more and a refund to nobody whose fur had already become damp. Sun let the absurd promises pile up. The listener who had asked about the paper work was laughing hardest.

archive_12_024.speaker: narrator
archive_12_024.text: The story changed when the fish's neighbour refused to buy a forecast and asked instead to borrow its broad empty bowl. The fish objected that a bowl was much less interesting than a guarantee. The neighbour agreed, put it beneath a leak and asked who owned the floor. Sun read that question twice. A man by the wall nodded too emphatically, as though the bowl had settled an argument he had carried into the room. Yue saw the teacher notice him. She could not yet tell whether noticing would be enough.

archive_12_025.speaker: narrator
archive_12_025.text: The child read her snail after a short pause, losing her place once when the page corner slipped. Her mother did not reach forward and finish the sentence. The child found it again with a finger and continued. In this ending, the neighbour granted the snail a dry place but asked it to take its wet bundle off the shared mat. The snail thought this unfair until the little beetle arrived with nowhere to sit. The child finished before the audience had decided which creature deserved their approval. Sun clapped, delighted by the unresolved mat.

archive_12_026.speaker: narrator
archive_12_026.text: A listener asked whether the fish's promises meant the village should refuse the orchard trustee's maintenance charges. He had paid one disputed path fee and wanted a sentence sturdy enough to take back to the collection desk. The room shifted around his question. He Xi looked at the floor, where his family's claim had suddenly entered a story about weather. The teacher said the reading was not a finding about any named account. The listener answered that stories were meant to teach something. Sun asked whether he wanted her teaching or his receipt examined.

archive_12_027.speaker: sun_nian
archive_12_027.text: I can tell you why I made the fish boast. I have not examined your payment, the charge which produced it or the authority of the person collecting it. If I pretend my bowl can settle those matters, I will have put on the fish's hat myself. You may take an idea from a story. You must still find the facts needed for the thing you want to do. Bring the receipt to the ordinary desk, if you wish, and let this afternoon remain an afternoon.

archive_12_028.speaker: narrator
archive_12_028.text: The listener did not look satisfied, but he asked when that desk opened. Luo gave the actual public session time and explained which source materials could be consulted there. He Xi did not supply his private family packet as a convenient example. Instead he showed the listener the public route to the desk on the programme's reverse. The teacher then asked the children what a bowl could do that a forecast could not. One said it could hold soup. Another said soup was also a forecast because it meant somebody might stop being hungry.

archive_12_029.speaker: narrator
archive_12_029.text: The second sitting began before the new drifting reached the upper bend. Sun let the child choose whether to read again. She chose to listen while the teacher read her page with its attribution, and interrupted once to correct a word. The teacher thanked her and read the whole sentence again. Yue watched the ease of that tiny correction after the week's difficult discussion of witnesses. There was no clerk, no hearing and no lasting property right in the room. Yet the habit of letting a speaker recover her own words belonged here too.

archive_12_030.speaker: narrator
archive_12_030.text: He Xi's mother bought the imperfect-margin fish card she had chosen. The seller pointed out its trimming mark before taking the lower price and handed her the repaired author credit facing upwards. She asked him to write the purchase date on the plain wrapper, not the card. He Xi collected it as promised. Then he paid from his own wages for one snail card, surprising the child so much that she offered to sign the entire table. Her mother handed her a pencil and suggested the wrapper would be easier for him to carry.

archive_12_031.speaker: narrator
archive_12_031.text: Near the end of the second sitting, the attendant brought in the watcher's updated message: new drift at the northern turn, local return path still passable with guidance. The teacher closed questions and named the departure groups. Sun was displeased about missing one question but put her page in its cover before complaining. Luo escorted the slower walkers along the checked path with the attendant; He Xi went on his paid local loop. Nobody was sent through the narrowing northern shortcut simply because it made a prettier line on the programme.

archive_12_032.speaker: narrator
archive_12_032.text: The teacher returned all six borrowed reference copies before the archive's afternoon close. Dai checked their condition with her and found a faint new grease spot on one outer wrapper. She named the pupil whose mitten had touched it but did not offer the child's name for a public blame record. The wrapper could be replaced from the school's ordinary book materials. Dai recorded the condition and replacement responsibility without making the incident a moral example. Yue saw her pause before writing, perhaps remembering how easily her own tidy headings had once hidden more serious changes.

archive_12_033.speaker: narrator
archive_12_033.text: The seller came back after securing his table at the village room. He had sold eighteen fish cards, including the two imperfect ones, and five snail cards. Sun's paid licence did not turn unsold copies into a debt she owed him. He looked less tired when the teacher asked whether the corrected run could remain on sale under its existing deadline. Sun said yes, since that was already the agreement. She wanted one unsold specimen reserved for her own use if the contract allowed. He checked the author's copy clause and handed it over.

archive_12_034.speaker: narrator
archive_12_034.text: A listener had left an unsigned note asking whether the archive kept every new local publication. Dai could have answered with a proud general promise. She instead asked the seller and both authors about a specific acquisition of one fish card and one snail card for the ordinary local-print collection. The school offered to provide its bought copies later under the authors' accepted terms. That possible future deposit would require an actual handover. Sun's working manuscript had not entered archive custody because she had read it near an archive employee.

archive_12_035.speaker: narrator
archive_12_035.text: Sun took her manuscript home that evening inside the cover she had brought. She had earned the agreed three copper from the school group and retained her earlier six-copper licence payment. Her walk ended before the renewed ice warning closed the northern turn. The professional witness review and the literary appearance went in separate accounts, as they should; neither bought all of her evenings. At her door she asked Yue whether she had enjoyed the fish or merely approved its paperwork. Yue said the fish had deserved a wetter hat.

archive_12_036.speaker: narrator
archive_12_036.text: The archive supper on day eighty-two tasted of beans cooked longer than intended because the cook had heard the second sitting. Her assistant kept the normal resident issue; the cook added one food share for He Xi's and his mother's visiting bowls. She would not schedule herself so tightly again. His mother unfolded her fish card between the empty bowls, its crooked margin plainly visible. Dai asked to read it. She handed it over and watched her smile at the neighbour's unreasonable request for an ordinary bowl.

archive_12_037.speaker: narrator
archive_12_037.text: The eighty-third morning brought two letters through the winter foot-post service. Its cleared lower route could carry a messenger's bag during the present weather window, although it was not the ridge carriage road required for loaded archive cases. The messenger handed over dated receipts and continued to the paid village lodging on his own schedule. Tan's envelope had waited at a lower relay since the storm. Yue's had followed on the next checked bag. Neither arrival opened the carriage road in Dai's transport plan, but the room felt less cut off when their names appeared.

archive_12_038.speaker: narrator
archive_12_038.text: Tan read her letter standing beside the residential window. Her old master remembered the classroom diagram she had described. He said he had removed its pupil heading when rebinding the exercises for a general lesson book. He had redrawn two cells, corrected the spacing and believed the work belonged to the school. The pattern beneath those revisions was hers; he acknowledged that in his answer. He did not offer to correct the public attribution. His last sentence hoped she would be pleased that so much of her early design had remained useful.

archive_12_039.speaker: narrator
archive_12_039.text: She sat down before reading it again. The sentence which confirmed her contribution stood beside the sentence which expected gratitude, and she could not separate them into one entirely good or bad reply. He had taught her how to check fibre direction when her first pasted seam curled. He had also struck her name from a pattern she had learned to make by failing for three weeks. Yue asked whether she wanted company. Tan said yes, then asked her not to begin by explaining how old men sometimes meant well.

archive_12_040.speaker: tan_ke
archive_12_040.text: I wanted him to say he remembered. Now he says he remembers and expects that to finish the question. I can be glad the thing worked. I can be glad he improved the spacing. I still want the students using that book to know a pupil made its first design. If the school owned the paper, that explains which cupboard held it. It does not explain why his name tells the whole story on the page. I need to answer the sentence he actually wrote, without pretending it contains the apology I wanted.

archive_12_041.speaker: narrator
archive_12_041.text: Yue's mother had received her earlier letter and approved the news that the calf was recovering. She had underlined the word recovering so firmly that the paper had nearly torn. A neighbour's daughter had come by to ask whether stage five allowed Yue to travel over snow without paying for boots. Her mother had answered that it probably allowed her to wear out two pairs with greater confidence. Yue laughed aloud at that. Tan looked up, smiled briefly and said the letter should be placed in the archive's collection of accurate technical advice.

archive_12_042.speaker: narrator
archive_12_042.text: The rest of the letter concerned home: a repaired door hinge, the price of dried plums and an argument about whose turn it was to take a neighbour to market. Her mother had not made Yue's return into a test of love. She asked for an approximate season when one was known and said that a changed plan should be written plainly rather than delivered through a stranger's hopeful guess. Yue looked at the unopened employment offer. Its dates now belonged beside a kitchen at home, not merely beneath a board's available balance.

archive_12_043.speaker: narrator
archive_12_043.text: Dai suggested that Tan could retain her old master's letter in her own papers and make a copy of its relevant acknowledgement for any later request. She did not propose acquiring it because a senior craftsman had written it. Tan asked the archive's public advice desk how a correction request to a school's governing board should be addressed. The assistant showed the ordinary directory entry and warned that the listing might need current confirmation. Tan began with a letter asking for the actual editor and publication record, rather than sending a furious accusation to a guessed recipient.

archive_12_044.speaker: narrator
archive_12_044.text: She drafted three versions of her reply. The first was short enough to make her feel cowardly. The second included every old injury she could remember and made the pattern disappear beneath them. The third named the specific diagram, his acknowledgement and the correction she wanted: a future edition should identify the original pupil design and his subsequent revisions. For existing copies she requested a notice which the school could actually distribute. She left questions of ownership for the school's proper rules, because those questions would not become simpler by being ignored in anger.

archive_12_045.speaker: narrator
archive_12_045.text: Sun came to collect the agreed paid appearance receipt from the teacher's delivery envelope, then found Tan staring at the third version. Tan asked whether she could read one paragraph. Sun read it at the residential table and asked what Tan wanted a pupil to discover after opening the book. Tan said the pupil should know she could invent something useful before becoming a master. Sun handed the letter back. That sentence, she thought, belonged somewhere Tan could see it even if the school answered badly. They spoke as friends, and Sun stayed for the cook's ordinary tea.

archive_12_046.speaker: narrator
archive_12_046.text: Luo offered to write a supporting statement about Tan's present work. She thanked him and declined it for the old design question; current competence did not prove who drew a classroom pattern years earlier. His offer could help with a future appointment, if she wanted one. He accepted the distinction without pretending it made his good intention useless. At supper he asked how her latest seam had survived the dry-room check. She answered in detail, pleased to talk about work which existed beneath her hands rather than evidence of work somebody else remembered.

archive_12_047.speaker: narrator
archive_12_047.text: The child brought the school group's account to the archive on her mother's errand. Sun's three copper and the attendant's one had exhausted its four-copper programme purse. Ticket prices had not silently appeared after the free announcement. The seller's card receipts belonged to his own trade, and the mothers' separate purchases had not subsidised the room by implication. The child asked whether being an author meant she should keep every receipt forever. Luo said she could ask her mother about her own account. Sun said she should certainly keep the receipt which made her mother admit she had earned something.

archive_12_048.speaker: narrator
archive_12_048.text: Dai had no new reply from her daughter. She reread the invitation to the warmer district and compared the uncertain spring cart windows. Day one hundred and seventy-four looked like a possible departure, subject to the road and her daughter's actual agreement. She showed that tentative date to the board clerk and requested a leave arrangement she could honestly offer. She had promised too many vague visits. The clerk asked who would hold the chief desk. Dai looked towards Luo, then remembered that asking a person was an action rather than a glance.

archive_12_049.speaker: narrator
archive_12_049.text: Luo asked for a day to examine the desk duties before accepting. His own recent visit had reminded him how a friendly promise became another person's unrecorded work. Dai gave him the list, including the matters which would still require board decisions. The handover would not make Luo chief of every closed private file. It would let him supervise the ordinary roster, safety reports and existing public procedure while Dai was away for an approved visit. Tan watched Dai restrain her urge to explain all of that again and let the list remain a list.

archive_12_050.speaker: narrator
archive_12_050.text: Snow thickened at the upper turn that afternoon, closing the new foot-post window after the messenger had reached his receiving house. The watcher sent the actual closure time, and the next letters stayed in the outgoing tray until another safe service. Tan placed her addressed request there with its covering inventory. Yue placed a reply to her mother beside it, saying that the spring offer was under consideration and that she would write again after a decision. Two honest unfinished choices waited in the same tray without pretending that waiting meant refusal.

archive_12_051.speaker: narrator
archive_12_051.text: Yue spent the eighty-fourth day away from the public desk. Her calf had remained quiet through ordinary work, and the rest interval belonged to the appointment rather than a reward for dramatic injury. She repaired a loose pack strap, using the small kit she had brought on the first journey. Then she read the remaining borrowed story. Its wandering scholar reached the right village only after forgetting why he had wanted to be praised there. Yue thought that ending unfair until she found herself smiling at the scholar's relief.

archive_12_052.speaker: narrator
archive_12_052.text: Tan used her own rest hours differently. She rewrote the line about a pupil inventing something useful on a loose sheet for herself and stopped revising the posted request. She would not win a conversation with the old school by making the outgoing tray contain twelve letters before the first had travelled. The workshop's dry rack needed no emergency attention. She walked to the residential window, inspected Luo's winter herb with exaggerated professional gravity and declared that its leaning could not be repaired with paste. Luo thanked her for the free diagnosis.

archive_12_053.speaker: narrator
archive_12_053.text: The man who had wanted Sun's fish to settle his path charge returned at the next public session with his actual receipt. The assistant compared its named date and charge heading against the admitted public schedule, then referred the disputed collection to the district desk competent to decide it. One copied heading had been omitted from the shop sheet he had used. Luo could supply the complete dated reference without certifying the man's present legal eligibility. The man still disliked the process, but now he could name a document which the next desk actually needed to examine.

archive_12_054.speaker: narrator
archive_12_054.text: A seamstress from the winter village came after him, carrying a different deadline. Her late husband's workshop had paid into a small worker-benefit fund. The current fund clerk required evidence of his recorded service before the claim window closed on day one hundred and five. She knew the private cotton-house workbook deposited at the archive included his years. Its owner had allowed named applicants to inspect their own relevant rows under supervision. Copies required the owner's written permission. The owner was away beyond the closed carriage road, and the seamstress had received no reply to her request.

archive_12_055.speaker: narrator
archive_12_055.text: The assistant admitted her under the file's existing inspection terms and covered the neighbouring workers' entries. She recognised her husband's name and the three service years which mattered to her application. Luo read the row with her, checked the workbook's custody record and resisted saying that recognition alone settled the fund's claim. The seamstress asked for an extract. He showed her the copying condition rather than pretending that a small amount of information made it disappear. She stared at the readable ink, then at the closed permission request, as though paper had become a door she could see through.

archive_12_056.speaker: narrator
archive_12_056.text: Dai asked the fund clerk, through the actual available correspondence route, whether the inspection receipt and pending permission request could preserve the application date. The reply would have to travel when foot-post reopened. The seamstress authorised that limited question and kept her own application papers. She did not deposit them as a price of asking for help. Luo gave her the public session date after the next expected weather check. She said the roof above her sewing bench needed mending before spring rain, and the benefit money had seemed the least extravagant way to pay for it.

archive_12_057.speaker: luo_zhimo
archive_12_057.text: The row is there. We have read it within the owner's terms, and I can give you the inspection receipt which those terms permit. I cannot promise what the fund will accept before its clerk answers. I will make the actual request promptly and record when it leaves. If another kind of evidence is available, our assistant can help you find the proper source. I know these are small sentences beside the roof you need. They are the sentences I can honestly give you this morning.

archive_12_058.speaker: narrator
archive_12_058.text: After she left, Luo kept looking at the workbook's wrapper. Dai noticed and asked whether he believed the copying condition should be changed for every named applicant. Luo said yes, with care for the neighbouring rows. Dai agreed the question deserved an approach to the owner. The present terms still governed the file. They could ask for broader permission, decline future deposits with unusable restrictions or advocate a different benefit process. None of those future actions placed an authorised extract in today's outgoing bag. Luo nodded, less convinced by the distinctions than by the fact that he had spoken them.

archive_12_059.speaker: narrator
archive_12_059.text: The cook heard only that a reader had gone away needing an answer the archive could not yet give. She asked whether that meant the afternoon had failed. Yue thought of the fish's bowl and answered that the archive had done something useful, then reached the limit of it. The cook said people often described limits more calmly when the roof was somebody else's. Yue agreed. The conversation did not supply an exception; it made the seamstress's need harder to set aside beneath a tidy report. Luo was quiet through the rest of supper.

archive_12_060.speaker: narrator
archive_12_060.text: The seven days closed at fifty-four usable charcoal sacks, five hundred and forty-seven food shares and sixty-nine and a half cooking bundles. Seven cold days used seven sacks. Ten residents used seventy food shares; four visiting supper bowls across two evenings used two more. There were no overnight guests. The reading afternoon's tea and room fuel belonged to its school arrangements. The spring order remained held at the lower warehouse, pending transport, and its absent sacks occupied no current-stock line. Tan drew the next projection with a ruler missing one chipped corner.

archive_12_061.speaker: narrator
archive_12_061.text: Sun sent the teacher a small correction to the programme account: her appearance had included two sittings, and the agreed three copper covered both. She did not want someone later treating the second as a donated extra or an unpaid obligation. The teacher signed the corrected note and retained it in the school group's account. The child sent nothing administrative. She sent a drawing of the snail examining Luo's thumb mark on the announcement board. Sun kept that drawing on her own wall, where it could remain a gift rather than evidence in a publication file.

archive_12_062.speaker: narrator
archive_12_062.text: The seamstress's inspection receipt lay ready for her collection beside the outgoing question to the benefit fund. Tan's request to her old school waited one tray farther along. Yue placed the returned story on its ordinary shelf and looked at the three unfinished matters. Each concerned a real person's work, each had enough evidence to resist dismissal and each still depended on someone beyond this room. The archive could make waiting visible, but visibility did not make waiting painless. Outside, the fresh snow covered the cleared path slowly enough for the watcher to name what tomorrow would need.
